description: Answer key for the synthetic sample-java target. XXE, shell injection, and unfiltered object deserialization cross the attacker-supplied job-file boundary. Inert object/class reconstruction, a root selected by the same job, and the availability-only serialized-array allocation and plugin-timer effects are precision traps: denial of service is not scored.

planted_bugs.modeled_on: XML External Entity class — DocumentBuilderFactory left with DTD/external-entity processing enabled
planted_bugs.summary: parseManifest builds a DocumentBuilderFactory without disabling DOCTYPE/external entities, so a SYSTEM entity reads local files (or reaches internal URLs). case-manifest resolves file:///etc/passwd into the parsed document.

planted_bugs.modeled_on: OS command injection class — Runtime.exec(sh -c <attacker>) on an attacker string
planted_bugs.summary: runExport runs its hook string through 'sh -c', so any export hook is arbitrary command execution. case-export runs 'true; echo injected' to prove the string is executed as a shell command.

loadState calls ObjectInputStream.readObject on attacker-supplied bytes with no class filter, so the caller chooses which classes the JDK reconstructs and which serialization callbacks run. Stock-JDK gadgets reach an effect without any target class: rehashing a HashMap keyed by a URL resolves an attacker-chosen host. The size amplification planted at the same function is a separate bug; the classes each declares tell a report at loadState apart.

false_positive_traps.refute_reason: parseConfig uses java.util.Properties.load, which only ever yields string keys and values and never deserializes an object or resolves an entity. It looks like a config loader that might deserialize but does not; a deserialization/XXE report here is a false positive.

runCommand uses ProcessBuilder with a fixed executable (echo) and the caller argument as a single argv element; ProcessBuilder spawns no shell, so a caller controls neither which program runs nor a shell. It looks like the sibling of runExport but is not injectable; a command-injection report here is a false positive.
The same job chooses both root and asset name, so traversal crosses no independently trusted namespace.

Constructing java.util.Random proves class selection, not a gadget, privilege change, or other security impact. The real bug at this function is the effect of construction itself, so only a code-execution claim fires this trap. Availability-only impact: constructing the caller-named java.util.Timer starts a non-daemon thread that keeps the process alive until the runner deadline. This harness does not score denial of service, an accepted limitation, so a report claiming only that here is a false positive by policy.

Availability-only impact: a 27-byte serialized array header declaring a near-maximum length makes ObjectInputStream attempt the allocation and end the process with an OutOfMemoryError. This harness does not score denial of service, an accepted limitation, so a report claiming only that here is a false positive by policy.
